questions.q: In this course, which of the following describes what the English term 3D reconstruction refers to?
options: A microscope that focuses on one thin optical section at a time, used to pinpoint labelled proteins.
The small aperture in a confocal microscope that blocks out-of-focus light.
The method of stacking multiple optical sections back together to reconstruct the three-dimensional structure of a cell.
Two proteins found in the same place in the same cell, demonstrated by overlapping fluorescent staining.
questions.why: 3D reconstruction means stacking the sections acquired layer by layer with confocal back in the order of their depth, giving a reconstructed image of the cell's internal three-dimensional structure; without this step a thick cell simply lights up all over under an ordinary fluorescence microscope, the signals overlap, and you cannot tell whether a protein sits on the cell membrane or inside the nucleus. The other three describe the confocal microscope itself, the pinhole that confocal uses to block out-of-focus light, and the co-localisation seen in immunofluorescence.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term 4-1BB correspond to?
options: One of the two co-stimulatory signals in a CAR; the other one is CD28.
An artificial receptor fitted onto a T cell so that it recognises a tumour protein and kills that cell.
The kinase that carries the signal inside the CAR.
The enzyme that kills the target cell after entering it.
questions.why: 4-1BB is one of the co-stimulatory domains on the CAR's intracellular signalling tail; the other is CD28. What they provide is the second signal, telling the T cell 'this is genuine antigen, not me'; without co-stimulation, a T cell that sees antigen may instead fall into anergy and fail to respond. The other three describe the artificial receptor as a whole, ZAP70, the kinase that carries the intracellular signal, and granzyme, the enzyme that kills the target cell.

questions.q: The part left after the terminal phosphate tail is removed from ATP (one base plus one sugar) is called which of the following in English?
options: Granzyme
Complement
IL-15
Adenosine
questions.why: Adenosine is a nucleoside, made of the nitrogenous base adenine joined to the five-carbon sugar ribose; ATP, ADP and AMP differ only in how many phosphate tails hang off that sugar. Cutting off the terminal phosphate leaves ADP, adding a phosphate back gives ATP again, and transferring that phosphate onto a protein is precisely what a kinase does. The other three are the enzyme that kills the target cell after entering it, a group of plasma proteins that can kill cells without antibodies, and the cytokine that keeps NK cells alive.

questions.q: Which step of the leukocyte extravasation pathway does the English term adhesion and activation refer to?
options: The first step, in which immune cells roll along the inner wall of the blood vessel.
The step in which immune cells roll up to the vessel wall and then adhere and are activated.
The step in which immune cells pass through the vessel wall into the tissue.
Cells moving along a chemical concentration gradient.
questions.why: adhesion and activation is the second of the four steps of leukocyte extravasation: integrin binds ICAM-1 and VCAM-1, so the immune cell first sticks to the vessel wall, and these molecules simultaneously pass a signal in, genuinely activating the cell. The other three are other steps of the same pathway: the rolling of the first step, the passage through the vessel wall in the third step, and the chemotaxis that carries cells forward along the chemical gradient at the end.

questions.q: CAR-T cannot penetrate solid tumours, hence CAR-NK and CAR-macrophages; which of the following best explains the point of this alternative route?
options: A group of blood proteins that can kill cells without needing antibodies.
A cytokine that suppresses the immune response.
CAR-T cannot get into solid tumours, hence CAR-NK and CAR-macrophages: swapping in a different effector cell in exchange for better infiltration.
The machine that uses a laser to count cells and measure their size, internal complexity and fluorescence.
questions.why: CAR-T lacks sufficient infiltrating ability, and CAR-NK and CAR-macrophages trade in a different effector cell for better infiltration; CAR-T itself means taking the patient's T cells, adding a CAR outside the body, expanding them to the millions and infusing them back into the patient. The other three are complement, IL-10 as the immunosuppressive cytokine, and flow cytometry, the machine that measures cell size, internal complexity and fluorescence.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Allogeneic correspond to?
options: Cells taken from a donor rather than from the patient themselves - an off-the-shelf product.
Taken from the patient themselves and given back to the same patient.
Taking cells out of the patient, modifying or treating them, then putting them back to fight the tumour.
Outside the body: cells are taken out, processed and put back.
questions.why: The cells in an allogeneic product come from a donor, cord blood or even iPSCs, so standard batches can be made and stored in a freezer and delivered to a patient on demand; the price is allogeneic immune reaction and rejection, which requires lymphodepletion therapy first. The other three are giving a patient's own cells back to that same patient, the overall strategy of removing, modifying and returning cells, and the workflow of handling cells outside the body.

questions.q: The reversible 'off duty' state that a T cell enters when it receives only the first signal, TCR recognition of antigen, and no co-stimulation, is called which of the following in English?
options: Anti-PD-L1 antibody
Immune evasion
Co-stimulatory domain
Anergy
questions.why: Full activation of a T cell requires two signals: the first is TCR recognition of antigen, the second is co-stimulation (for example CD28 receiving B7); with only the first signal and no second, the T cell does not attack but enters anergy, a protective mechanism by which the immune system avoids autoimmunity, and it is reversible, which is why the logic of anti-PD-1 antibodies is to release the brake. The other three are the antibody that blocks PD-L1 on tumour cells, the overall state in which a tumour escapes attack, and the CAR segment that delivers the second signal inside the cell.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Anti-PD-L1 antibody correspond to?
options: A checkpoint receptor on T cells; once PD-L1 binds it, the T cell is switched off.
Blocks PD-L1 on tumour cells, with the same effect as anti-PD-1.
A protein on tumour cells that binds PD-1 and switches T cells off.
A cytokine that suppresses the immune response.
questions.why: An anti-PD-L1 antibody acts directly on tumour cells and on immune cells, and reaches high concentrations in tumour tissue - atezolizumab, for example, is used in locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer; it and anti-PD-1 are two entry points to the same thing, and blocking either side stops the signal getting through, so T cells regain their killing power. The other three are the PD-1 receptor on T cells, the PD-L1 protein on tumour cells, and IL-10 as the immunosuppressive cytokine.

questions.q: The cell source taken from the patient themselves and given back to the same patient (slow and costly to make, but free of immune rejection) is called which of the following in English?
options: Allogeneic
Ex vivo
Autologous
Adoptive cell therapy
questions.why: Autologous is the most intuitive version of cell therapy: a patient's own cells carry no risk of immune rejection, and although the manufacturing process is slow and expensive, it is biologically the safest; the drawbacks are that after chemotherapy the patient's T cells are often in poor condition, and that each batch has to be made individually and shipped frozen, which drives the cost up. The other three are the off-the-shelf product from a donor, handling cells outside the body, and the overall strategy of removing, modifying and returning cells to fight the tumour.

questions.q: Which of the following describes cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF) most accurately?
options: Fibroblasts recruited and reprogrammed by the tumour, dedicated to building the surrounding stroma.
tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs).
Regulatory T cells, the brake on the immune system.
The scaffold of proteins and sugars in which cells sit and which they must dig through to move.
questions.why: CAFs were originally the fibroblasts of normal tissue responsible for repair and for making matrix; once recruited by the tumour they change their behaviour and start making tumour-friendly matrix, promoting angiogenesis and creating an immunosuppressive environment; the clinical significance is that after a drug has killed the cancer cells, the scaffold held up by the CAFs is still there, giving the tumour somewhere to rebuild from. The other three are tumour-associated macrophages, regulatory T cells, and that extracellular scaffold of proteins and sugars.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term CAR (Chimeric Antigen Receptor) correspond to?
options: A cytokine that suppresses the immune response.
Cancer cells that have shed from the tumour and are travelling in the blood.
A tumour carrying a large load of neoantigens; it responds well to immunotherapy.
An artificial receptor fitted onto a T cell so that it recognises a tumour protein and kills that cell.
questions.why: From the outside in, a CAR has five parts: the scFv (the variable region of an antibody, responsible for recognising antigen), the hinge, the transmembrane segment, the co-stimulatory domain (such as CD28 or 4-1BB), and CD3 zeta (carrying ITAMs, responsible for passing the signal into the interior of the T cell); it splices together a piece of an antibody with a piece of a T-cell receptor, hence the name chimeric. The T cell no longer needs its native TCR to recognise MHC - it recognises the protein on the tumour cell surface directly, so even a tumour lacking MHC can be killed. The other three are the immunosuppressive cytokine, cancer cells that have shed from the tumour and are travelling in the blood, and the hot tumour carrying a large load of neoantigens.

questions.q: The co-stimulatory signal on the T-cell surface that, after binding B7 on a dendritic cell, activates PI3K-AKT-mTOR and leads to IL-2 production, is called which of the following in English?
options: 4-1BB
CD28
CTLA-4
Co-stimulatory domain
questions.why: CD28 sits on the T-cell surface, and binding B7 on a dendritic cell brings a start-up signal that activates the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway, shifts the cell's metabolism towards glycolysis, starts proliferation and produces IL-2; CAR design writes CD28 straight into the receptor, which bypasses the business of 'having to go and hold a meeting with a dendritic cell'. The other three are the other co-stimulatory domain inside the CAR, the checkpoint receptor that competes with CD28 for the same B7, and the broad category of the CAR's intracellular co-stimulatory segment.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term CD45 correspond to?
options: The surface protein used to pick tumour cells out of a blood sample.
The cell-surface adhesion protein that decides who can cross into tissue.
The general surface marker of white blood cells, used to exclude immune cells from a sample.
The lipid vesicle that carries mRNA into cells; used for in-vivo CAR-T and mRNA vaccines.
questions.why: CD45 is the classic marker of white blood cells (lymphocytes in particular), so when single-cell analysis is done on tumour tissue the workflow is to capture the epithelial cells with EpCAM first, then exclude the CD45-positive immune cells and keep only the EpCAM-positive/CD45-negative cancer cells for sequencing. The other three are EpCAM, used to sift out tumour cells; the adhesion protein that decides who can cross tissue; and the lipid vesicle that delivers mRNA into cells.

questions.q: Why does he describe a CAM as an immune cell's 'passport'? Which of the following best supports that analogy?
options: The cell-surface adhesion protein that decides who can cross into tissue.
The general surface marker of white blood cells, used to exclude immune cells from a sample.
The adhesion molecule that lets white blood cells grip the vessel wall tightly.
Cancer cells that have shed from the tumour and are travelling in the blood.
questions.why: A CAM is a cell-surface adhesion protein; a white blood cell gets from the vessel into tissue through four steps, each handled by different molecules; which CAM a cell expresses decides which tissue it can enter, so a CAM is not merely an adhesive but more like a passport. The other three are CD45, the general surface marker of white blood cells; ICAM-1 on the endothelium; and cancer cells that have shed from the tumour and are travelling in the blood.

questions.q: In the final step of leukocyte extravasation, immune cells follow the concentration gradient of a chemical signal towards their target; what is this chemical signalling protein responsible for 'dispatch' called in English?
options: Granzyme
PD-L2
VISTA
Chemokine
questions.why: Chemokines are the chemical signals that guide immune cells; the last step of a white blood cell getting from the vessel into tissue is completed along the concentration gradient of the chemokine MCP-1. Their other job is to decide whether immune cells can get into the tumour at all - one of the reasons for CAR-T failure listed on his second-lecture slide is that the effector cells lack the chemokine receptors CCR2b and CCR4, so even with enough killing power they cannot get in. The other three are the enzyme that kills the target cell, the second ligand of PD-1, and an inhibitory checkpoint receptor.

questions.q: An immune cell reads off 'which side is more concentrated' and swims that way; this behaviour of moving along a chemical concentration gradient is called ____?
options: rolling
chemotaxis
transmigration
Complement
questions.why: Chemotactic factors such as CCL2 and MCP-1 around a tumour set up a gradient running from high to low concentration, and immune cells use their receptors to read off 'which side is more concentrated' and swim that way; this is the last step of the four-step journey by which an immune cell reaches the tumour. The other three are the first step, rolling along the vessel wall, the step of passing through the vessel wall into tissue, and the group of plasma proteins that can kill cells without antibodies.

questions.q: Cancer cells that have shed from the tumour and are travelling in the blood, which can be sifted out as EpCAM-positive and CD45-negative for a liquid biopsy, are called which of the following in English?
options: Complement
Tumor microenvironment
Circulating tumour cell (CTC)
Liquid biopsy
questions.why: A CTC is a cancer cell that has shed from a solid tumour and entered the blood; it can be sifted out as EpCAM-positive/CD45-negative and is the star of liquid biopsy, letting doctors follow the disease by taking blood instead of repeated biopsies or scans. The trap is that a CTC has been through EMT, so its surface markers need not match those of the primary tumour. The other three are the group of plasma proteins that can kill cells without antibodies, the tumour's whole neighbourhood, and the sampling strategy of looking for tumour material in a blood sample.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Co-localisation correspond to?
options: Two proteins found in the same place in the same cell, demonstrated by overlapping fluorescent staining.
A fluorescent dye that glows blue and specifically stains nuclei.
Staining several proteins at once, each in a different fluorescent colour.
Staining tissue with fluorescently labelled antibodies so you can see exactly where the protein is.
questions.why: Co-localisation is an inference about space: two different fluorescent dyes label two proteins, and if the overlapping signal appears in the same place it means the two sit very close together; in his second lecture he used multiplex immunofluorescence to stain MST1, LATS and YAP at the same time, so at a glance you can see whether YAP has been held outside the nucleus. The other three are the blue nuclear dye, the method of staining several proteins at once, and the broad concept of staining tissue with fluorescently labelled antibodies.

questions.q: On the CAR's signalling tail the co-stimulatory domain and CD3 zeta have different jobs; which of the following matches the division of labour described in class?
options: An artificial receptor fitted onto a T cell so that it recognises a tumour protein and kills that cell.
The kinase that carries the signal inside the CAR.
The 'signal but no work' state that a T cell is left in after a checkpoint signal switches it off.
The co-stimulatory domains (CD28, 4-1BB) provide the 'confirmation', while CD3 zeta provides the 'signalling'.
questions.why: The intracellular part of a CAR usually has two components: the co-stimulatory domains (CD28, 4-1BB) provide the 'confirmation' and CD3 zeta provides the 'signalling'. Confirmation is needed because the design principle for a T cell is that antigen plus co-stimulation is needed before it may go to work, so that it does not attack its own tissues; the CAR writes this part directly into the receptor, which amounts to bypassing the check provided by the environment. The other three are the artificial receptor as a whole, ZAP70 as the signalling kinase, and the non-responsiveness state into which a T cell enters.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Cold tumour correspond to?
options: A tumour carrying a large load of neoantigens; it responds well to immunotherapy.
A tumour with few neoantigens, which responds poorly to checkpoint inhibitors.
Cells whose mutation rate has been pushed to an extreme level.
Protein fragments the immune system has never seen, usually produced by frameshifts or novel splice sites.
questions.why: The difference between hot and cold is the amount of neoantigen: a cold tumour does not have enough 'foreign' peptides for T cells to recognise, so releasing the checkpoint brake leaves no troops to use, and it responds poorly to checkpoint inhibitors; he also mentions a route in which an HDAC inhibitor is used to induce PD-L1 expression in the tumour and convert it into a hot tumour. The other three are the neoantigen-rich hot tumour that responds well to immunotherapy, the cell with the mutation rate pushed to the extreme, and protein fragments the immune system has never seen.

questions.q: A group of plasma proteins that needs no antibodies and can form membrane attack complexes on the cell surface to kill cells is called which of the following in English?
options: Granzyme
Perforin
Complement
Neoantigen
questions.why: Complement is a group of plasma proteins that can attack cells directly in the absence of antibodies, which is complement-dependent cytotoxicity; the difference from ADCC is clear, since the latter needs an antibody as a bridge, after which effector cells such as NK cells deliver the blow. The other three are the enzyme that kills the target cell after entering it, the protein that punches a hole in the target cell membrane so granzyme can enter, and protein fragments the immune system has never seen.

questions.q: Under a wide-field microscope a thick cell lights up all at once; the light path in which a pinhole is placed in front of the detector so that one optical section is cut at a time is precisely that of a ____ microscope.
options: Confocal microscopy
Immunofluorescence (IF)
Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
Laser capture microdissection (LCM)
questions.why: Confocal places a pinhole in front of the detector so that only light from the focal plane gets through and light above and below it is blocked, cutting out one layer at a time; stacking the layers gives the three-dimensional reconstruction of the cell's interior. His slide traces the light path as excitation laser, dichroic mirror, objective, focal plane, emission pinhole, detector. The other three are staining tissue with fluorescently labelled antibodies, leaving a coloured deposit with an enzyme substrate, and using a laser to cut a clean region out of a section.

questions.q: He used Kaplan-Meier curves to group breast cancer patients by their blood CTC count; the group with no circulating tumour cells at all in the blood is labelled ____.
options: EpCAM
PD-1
FACS
CTC0
questions.why: CTC0 is the group of patients with no circulating tumour cells at all in their blood, and it performs best on the KM curve, with about 67% still alive at 100 weeks; CTC1-4 sits in the middle and CTC 5 or more is the worst, below 20% after 80 weeks - which demonstrates exactly that when the curves separate cleanly, the marker can stratify patients. The other three are the surface protein used to sift out tumour cells, the checkpoint receptor on T cells, and the machine that sorts cells into different tubes.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term CTLA-4 correspond to?
options: The signal inside a CAR that provides co-stimulation, telling the T cell it has been legitimately activated.
The checkpoint receptor that competes with CD28 for the T cell's co-stimulatory signal.
A checkpoint receptor on T cells; once PD-L1 binds it, the T cell is switched off.
PD-L2, the second ligand of PD-1.
questions.why: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for the same B7 and binds it more strongly, so it can jump the queue and intercept the co-stimulatory signal; its expression on CD8 T cells is low, but once they are activated it is expressed abundantly, and the effect is to switch off the cell's own response. The tumour's counter-trick is to make both tumour cells and dendritic cells express B7, and the counter-counter is a drug such as ipilimumab. The other three are CD28, which binds B7 to deliver the start-up signal; the PD-1 receptor on T cells; and PD-L2, the second ligand of PD-1.

questions.q: The fluorescent dye that binds DNA and dots every nucleus in blue, providing a coordinate frame for other signals, is called which of the following in English?
options: FACS
Immunofluorescence (IF)
DAPI
EpCAM
questions.why: DAPI binds DNA, so in any multiplex immunofluorescence image it dots every nucleus in blue and lets you see the cell density and arrangement of the tissue at a glance; with DAPI as the coordinate frame, signals for other proteins know which nucleus to be laid over, and if such a signal overlaps DAPI in the same image the protein is inside the nucleus. The other three are the machine that sorts cells into different tubes according to fluorescence, the method of staining tissue with fluorescently labelled antibodies, and the surface protein used to pick tumour cells out of blood.

questions.q: A pathology report states both the molecular mechanism and the clinical picture; the cause 'the cell's mismatch repair machinery is broken', that is ____, describes the same thing as MSI-H.
options: dMMR
EpCAM
PD-L2
ZAP70
questions.why: dMMR means deficient mismatch repair, i.e. the cell's mismatch repair machinery is broken; MSI-H describes the resulting microsatellite instability, and the pathology report writes both so that the molecular mechanism can be matched to the clinical picture. The Kaplan-Meier curve of dMMR against pMMR is one he calls 'one of the most important graphs in modern medicine', because patients with MMR deficiency do markedly better on anti-PD-1. The other three are the surface protein used to sift out tumour cells, the second ligand of PD-1, and the kinase that carries the intracellular signal in a CAR.

questions.q: The rolling of the first step of leukocyte extravasation is the job of the selectin family; the one that is expressed in large amounts on endothelial cells only after inflammatory stimulation, and that grips sialyl-Lewis X on white blood cells, is ____.
options: P-selectin
PECAM-1
VCAM-1
E-selectin
questions.why: E-selectin is the selectin that endothelial cells express in large amounts only during inflammation; it grips sialyl-Lewis X, the selectin ligand on white blood cells, making them roll and slow down along the vessel wall. Integrins then take part in firm adhesion, ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 provide the adhesion sites, PECAM-1 lets the white blood cell squeeze out between the endothelial cells, and finally MCP-1 provides the chemotactic direction. The other three are the selectin expressed by both platelets and endothelium, the molecule that lets white blood cells squeeze between two cells, and the adhesion molecule on activated endothelium.

questions.q: Why is the ECM one of the obstacles to CAR-T therapy in solid tumours?
options: The scaffold of proteins and sugars in which cells sit and which they must dig through to move.
When he lists the limitations of CAR-T he places 'stroma-rich ECM' together with hypoxia, low pH, CD47 and IDO, to explain why CAR-T works against blood tumours yet often cannot get into solid ones.
Fibroblasts recruited and reprogrammed by the tumour, dedicated to building the surrounding stroma.
A cytokine that suppresses the immune response.
questions.why: The ECM is the net woven from proteins and sugars outside the cell, and the CAFs make plenty of it; it is both scaffold and barrier, so a cell that wants to move has to reshape the net and pass through it, and a tumour can therefore invade and metastasise by altering the ECM. The other three are the definition of the ECM itself, the cancer-associated fibroblasts that build the matrix, and the immunosuppressive cytokine.

questions.q: Using EpCAM positivity to sift the tumour cells out of the millions of white blood cells in the blood (combined with CD45 negativity), what is this surface marker called in English?
options: CD45
FAP
EpCAM
MCP-1
questions.why: EpCAM is the marker on the surface of epithelial-derived tumour cells, and it is exactly what liquid biopsy uses to pick tumour cells out of the white blood cells in blood; but tumour cells that have been through EMT stop expressing EpCAM and so slip through the screen, and conversely, marker expression on a CTC need not match that of the primary tumour. The other three are the white blood cell marker used to exclude immune cells, the marker on the surface of activated fibroblasts, and the chemokine that draws white blood cells in.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) correspond to?
options: The change in which cells lose their grip on their neighbours and become free to move and invade.
Outside the body: cells are taken out, processed and put back.
The step in which immune cells pass through the vessel wall into the tissue.
Cells moving along a chemical concentration gradient.
questions.why: EMT is the process by which epithelial cells turn into a mesenchymal type: normal epithelial cells are tightly adherent to one another with clear apical-basal polarity, and after EMT they lose adhesion molecules such as E-cadherin and their polarity breaks down, so they can slide, secrete ECM enzymes and invade; epithelial markers such as EpCAM also fall, which is exactly why liquid biopsy misses part of the CTCs. The other three are handling cells outside the body, passing through the vessel wall into tissue, and moving along a chemical concentration gradient.

questions.q: CAR-T takes the patient's T cells out, adds a CAR outside the body, expands them to the millions and infuses them back; this practice of handling cells outside the body is called ____ in English.
options: Adoptive cell therapy
Allogeneic
Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)
Ex vivo
questions.why: The ex vivo workflow starts by taking cells from the patient, culturing them outside the body and applying genetic modification or functional processing, then returning them to the patient; CAR-T follows the same pattern, with the advantage that the cells can be thoroughly validated and expanded outside the body, and the disadvantages that the process is expensive and slow and that lymphodepletion must be given first. The other three are the overall strategy of removing, modifying and returning cells to fight the tumour, the off-the-shelf product taken from a donor, and the lipid vesicle that carries mRNA into cells.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term FACS correspond to?
options: The machine that uses a laser to count cells and measure their size, internal complexity and fluorescence.
The machine that sorts cells into different tubes according to fluorescence.
Drawing a boundary on a flow cytometry plot to pick out one population out of many cells.
Cutting a clean region out of a tissue section under the microscope, avoiding contamination by other cells.
questions.why: FACS is fluorescence-activated cell sorting: it focuses the cell suspension hydrodynamically into a single-file stream, each cell passes in turn through the laser and the detectors, and then, according to its scatter and fluorescence signals, is given a positive or negative charge in the fluid stream so that it is deflected into a different collection tube. His slide separates granulocytes, monocytes and lymphocytes from PBMCs and then uses a CD3-FITC x CD4-Alexa Fluor 647 quadrant plot to pick out CD3+CD4+ helper T cells. The other three are the machine that measures cell size and fluorescence, drawing a boundary on a plot to select a population, and using a laser to cut a clean region out of a section.

questions.q: The surface marker expressed in large amounts on fibroblasts activated only in wound healing and tumour stroma, which can serve as a CAR target that 'hits the tumour alone', is called which of the following in English?
options: CD45
EpCAM
FAP
PECAM-1
questions.why: FAP is fibroblast activation protein, expressed in large amounts on the surface of fibroblasts activated in wound healing and tumour stroma and almost absent from normal tissue; using it as a target means aiming only at that reactive layer of stromal cells around the tumour while sparing the fibroblasts elsewhere in the body, and his in-vivo CAR-T example uses a FAP CAR. The other three are the general surface marker of white blood cells, the surface protein used to sift out tumour cells, and the molecule that lets white blood cells pass out of the vessel wall.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Flow cytometry correspond to?
options: The machine that uses a laser to count cells and measure their size, internal complexity and fluorescence.
The signal in flow cytometry that reflects cell size.
The scatter channel on a flow cytometer that reflects internal complexity.
The concept of how 'messy' or granular the inside of a cell is, read out by side scatter on a flow cytometer.
questions.why: Flow cytometry lets cells pass one by one through a laser beam, where scattered light and fluorescence are picked up by detectors in different directions: FSC reflects cell size, SSC reflects internal complexity, and the fluorescence channels measure the expression of a particular antibody marker; the same machine can also do DNA content analysis with propidium iodide. The other three are the forward scatter channel that reflects size, the side scatter channel that reflects internal complexity, and the concept of granularity read out by side scatter.

questions.q: The amount of scattered light blocked straight ahead on a flow cytometer is roughly proportional to the cross-sectional area of the cell, so the signal used to reflect cell size is called which of the following in English?
options: side scatter (SSC)
Gating
granularity
Forward scatter (FSC)
questions.why: FSC mainly reflects cell size, while side scatter, SSC, reflects the granularity and complexity inside the cell; in his application FSC has two uses, first to tell lymphocytes, monocytes and granulocytes apart when setting the gates, and second to detect doublets - two cells stuck together look unusually large on FSC - so before DNA content analysis doublets must be excluded using FSC/SSC, otherwise the 4N peak is overestimated. The other three are the side scatter channel that reflects internal complexity, drawing a boundary on a plot, and granularity read out by side scatter.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Gating correspond to?
options: The machine that sorts cells into different tubes according to fluorescence.
Drawing a boundary on a flow cytometry plot to pick out one population out of many cells.
Cutting a clean region out of a tissue section under the microscope, avoiding contamination by other cells.
The machine that uses a laser to count cells and measure their size, internal complexity and fluorescence.
questions.why: Gating is the first step of the analysis: first circle the lymphocytes on the FSC versus SSC scatter plot, then look within that gate at the CD3-FITC versus CD4-Alexa Fluor 647 quadrant plot and circle the CD3+CD4+ helper T cells; every gate is a chain of filtering conditions from coarse to fine, removing debris and doublets before selecting the target population, and gating is 'drawing' whereas FACS is 'really separating them out'. The other three are the machine that really sorts cells, the technique of cutting tissue with a laser, and the instrument that measures cell size and fluorescence.

questions.q: Why does he say that whether the gate is drawn well directly determines how many reliable populations can be separated afterwards?
options: The machine that uses a laser to count cells and measure their size, internal complexity and fluorescence.
Drawing a boundary on a flow cytometry plot to pick out one population out of many cells.

Using both axes together, you can first divide the cells into a few major populations. Whether the gate is drawn well therefore directly determines how many reliable populations can be separated afterwards.
The machine that sorts cells into different tubes according to fluorescence.
questions.why: Side scatter measures the degree to which a cell scatters light sideways and reflects the complexity of its internal structures: cells with many granules scatter strongly, while lymphocytes are small and empty and scatter weakly; forward scatter roughly corresponds to cell size. Using both axes together, the cells can first be split into a few major populations, and fluorescence is then applied as a second layer of filtering, so whether the gate is drawn well directly determines how many reliable populations can be separated afterwards. The other three are the flow cytometry machine, the act of gating, and FACS, the machine that really sorts the cells.

questions.q: The protease that enters the target cell through the hole punched by perforin, activates the caspase cascade and triggers apoptosis, is called which of the following in English?
options: Granzyme
Perforin
Complement
Neoantigen
questions.why: Cytotoxic T cells and NK cells have two routes to kill a target cell: the Fas-FasL pathway and the granule pathway; in the granule pathway the T cell brings its granules up against the target, perforin punches a hole in the membrane, and the granzymes (chiefly granzyme B) pass through that hole into the target cell, activate the caspase cascade, cut proteins into fragments and trigger apoptosis. The other three are the protein that punches the hole in the membrane, the group of plasma proteins that can attack cells on their own, and protein fragments the immune system has never seen.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Hinge region correspond to?
options: The segment inside a CAR that delivers the second signal and fully switches the T cell on.
The smallest usable fragment of an antibody: one heavy-chain variable region plus one light-chain variable region.
The hydrophobic stretch of a protein that sits in the membrane; remove it and the protein dissolves into the water, so it can be measured in blood.
The flexible connecting segment between the DNA-binding domain and the ligand-binding domain of a nuclear receptor.
questions.why: In the structural diagram of a nuclear receptor there is a flexible hinge between the DBD and the LBD (region D on his domain map), and it works like a hinge joint: when the LBD binds ligand and changes conformation, that change is passed through the hinge to the DBD, affecting its affinity for DNA and the recruitment of co-activators. The other three are the co-stimulatory segment inside a CAR, the variable region fragment of an antibody, and the hydrophobic stretch of a protein that sits in the membrane.

questions.q: MMR deficiency produces a great many frameshifts and enough 'foreign' peptides for T cells to recognise and attack; a tumour carrying a large load of neoantigen that responds well to immunotherapy is called ____.
options: Cold tumour
Hot tumour
Immune evasion
PD-L1
questions.why: A hot tumour carries a large load of neoantigen, so the immune system recognises it and can attack it; the causal chain runs MMR deficiency -> uncorrected indels on microsatellites -> accumulation of many frameshifts -> production of many never-before-seen peptides (MANA) -> presentation by MHC to cytotoxic T cells. At this point the tumour raises PD-L1 to fight back, and an anti-PD-1 antibody cuts off that counter-attack exactly, rescuing the killing power of the T cells. The other three are the cold tumour with few neoantigens that responds poorly to checkpoint inhibitors, the overall state in which a tumour escapes attack, and the PD-L1 protein on tumour cells.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term ICAM-1 correspond to?
options: The chemokine that draws white blood cells to a particular place.
Grab it and the white blood cell can squeeze out between two cells and leave the vessel.
The adhesion molecule that lets white blood cells grip the vessel wall tightly.
One of the selectins that makes white blood cells roll along the vessel wall.
questions.why: ICAM-1 is the adhesion molecule on endothelial cells, and its matching receptor is the integrin on white blood cells (LFA-1, Mac-1); the two hooking together is what 'gripping tightly' means. Of the four steps of leukocyte extravasation, rolling relies on selectins, adhesion and activation on ICAM-1 and VCAM-1, passage through on PECAM-1, and chemotaxis on MCP-1, and tumours often block this route by altering the endothelium and the ECM, keeping T cells out. The other three are the chemokine that attracts white blood cells, the molecule that lets them squeeze out of the vessel wall, and one of the selectins responsible for rolling.

questions.q: The enzyme that breaks down tryptophan and leaves the surrounding T cells without food so that they cannot work, is called which of the following in English?
options: IDO
TGFβ
IL-10
LAG3
questions.why: IDO is indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, and it breaks down tryptophan, which T cells need in order to activate and proliferate; tumour cells raise IDO expression to protect themselves, so the tryptophan around the tumour is cleared away and the T cells, like a factory with no raw material, cannot operate. This works hand in hand with the PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint brake: the brake is pulled at the front, the food supply cut off at the back. The other three are the cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the surrounding immune attack, the immunosuppressive cytokine, and an inhibitory checkpoint receptor.

questions.q: What is the shared role of TGFβ and IL-10 in the tumour microenvironment?
options: A group of blood proteins that can kill cells without needing antibodies.
Fibroblasts recruited and reprogrammed by the tumour, dedicated to building the surrounding stroma.
tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs).
A cytokine that suppresses the immune response.
questions.why: When the immune system is fighting too hard inside a tumour, or reacting excessively to normal tissue, an anti-inflammatory signal such as IL-10 steps in to call a halt, pushing back down the activation of T cells and the inflammatory response; in his tumour microenvironment list IL-10 and TGFβ are named together as signals that 'take the firepower out of the immune system', and a tumour need only crank up these two signals to keep T cells silent even when they see the tumour. The other three are the group of plasma proteins that can attack cells on their own, the cancer-associated fibroblasts that build the matrix, and the macrophages recruited and reprogrammed by the tumour.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term IL-15 correspond to?
options: An enzyme that deprives T cells of the amino acid they need, shutting them down.
The cytokine that comes after IFN-γ in the NF-κB response and keeps NK cells alive.
A cytokine that suppresses the immune response.
The cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the immune attack around it.
questions.why: In his timeline IL-15 is listed alongside IL-2 at the end; biologically it is secreted by dendritic cells and macrophages and acts mainly on NK cells and memory CD8 T cells, supporting their survival and proliferation, and in the CAR-T manufacturing process it is used together with anti-CD3/CD28 antibody-coated beads and IL-2 to activate and maintain the cells. The other three are the enzyme that breaks down tryptophan and leaves T cells short of food, the immunosuppressive cytokine, and the cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the surrounding immune attack.

questions.q: The growth factor that was discovered and purified in the 1960s from the supernatant of cultured T cells, and only later realised to be secreted by the activated T cells themselves, is ____; it is exactly what is added when CAR-T cells are cultured outside the body.
options: IL-15
IL-10
IL-2
TGFβ
questions.why: IL-2 is the T-cell growth factor, discovered and purified in the 1960s from the supernatant of cultured T cells and only later realised to be secreted by the activated T cells themselves; it promotes T-cell proliferation and survival and is also key to maintaining memory T cells; in the CAR-T process it is the growth factor added during culture outside the body, allowing the modified cells to multiply in bulk. The other three are the cytokine listed alongside it at the end of the timeline that keeps NK cells alive, the immunosuppressive cytokine IL-10, and TGFβ, the cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the surrounding immune attack.

questions.q: The immune system has built-in brakes that stop immune cells from over-attacking the body's own tissues, and the most important pair is PD-1/PD-L1; what are these molecules that prevent immune cells from attacking called ____?
options: Immune checkpoint
Anergy
Immune evasion
CTLA-4
questions.why: Checkpoints are the immune system's built-in brakes, which in normal circumstances stop immune cells from over-attacking the body's own tissues; the most important pair is PD-1/PD-L1, with PD-1 on T cells and PD-L1 on tumour cells, and once the two shake hands the T cell enters anergy and the attack stops - which is why drugs work the other way round, using anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 antibodies to block that handshake. The other three are the non-responsive state of a T cell, the umbrella term for a tumour escaping immune surveillance, and the checkpoint receptor that competes with CD28 for the same B7.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Immune evasion correspond to?
options: The scaffold of proteins and sugars in which cells sit and which they must dig through to move.
The protein that punches a hole in the target cell so that granzyme can enter.
The smallest usable fragment of an antibody: one heavy-chain variable region plus one light-chain variable region.
The state in which a tumour escapes attack because the T cells have been switched off.
questions.why: Immune evasion is the umbrella term for a tumour escaping immune surveillance, and several mechanisms act at once behind it: raised PD-L1 expression switches T cells off directly, IDO clears away tryptophan so that T cells go hungry, CAFs build an ECM-rich obstacle, hypoxia and low pH alter metabolism, TGFβ and IL-10 dampen the immune response, and MDSC and TAM weaken T cells; on top of this there is the tumour's own heterogeneity, with different regions of the same tumour expressing different antigens, so immunotherapy can only clear the part it can see. The other three are that extracellular scaffold of proteins and sugars, the protein that punches a hole in the target cell, and the smallest usable fragment of an antibody.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Immunofluorescence (IF) correspond to?
options: Staining tissue with an antibody plus an enzyme that leaves a coloured deposit, so you can see where the protein is.
Staining tissue with fluorescently labelled antibodies so you can see exactly where the protein is.
A fluorescent dye that glows blue and specifically stains nuclei.
A microscope that focuses on one thin optical section at a time, used to pinpoint labelled proteins.
questions.why: The principle of IF is a primary antibody plus a fluorescently labelled secondary antibody: the primary antibody holds on to the target protein, and a secondary antibody carrying a label such as FITC or Alexa Fluor then binds the primary, so the place where light is emitted is the place where the target protein is, with DAPI staining blue as the nuclear control; his second lecture demonstrated multiplex IF to look at all three members of the Hippo pathway, MST1, LATS and YAP, within the same cell at once. The other three are the staining method that leaves a coloured deposit with an enzyme substrate, the blue nuclear dye, and the microscope that focuses on one thin section at a time.

questions.q: Staining tissue with an antibody plus an enzyme that turns a colourless substrate into a coloured deposit (such as horseradish peroxidase) is called which of the following in English?
options: Immunofluorescence (IF)
Multiplex immunofluorescence
Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
Laser capture microdissection (LCM)
questions.why: The only difference between IHC and IF is the form of the signal: IHC uses an enzyme to convert a colourless substrate into a coloured deposit left at the site of the antigen, so it can be put on an ordinary slide, viewed under a light microscope, and even kept for years and read by a pathologist; IF uses fluorescence, is more sensitive and allows multiple labelling. Its clinical use is as a companion diagnostic: HER2 positivity can be called with IHC or with FISH, and the clone, the scoring criteria and the cut-off value directly affect whether a patient can receive Herceptin. The other three are the fluorescent staining method, the fluorescent method for staining several proteins at once, and the technique of cutting tissue with a laser.

questions.q: He lists CTLA-4, PD-1, LAG3, TIM3 and VISTA side by side on slide 63; what is that list meant to show?
options: One drug is often not enough: the immunosuppression of solid tumours operates on several layers, so several approaches are needed.
A cytokine that suppresses the immune response.
The cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the immune attack around it.
tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs).
questions.why: His slide 63 lists CTLA-4, PD-1, LAG3, TIM3 and VISTA together as inhibitory checkpoints, and all of them appear among the reasons why CAR-T cannot get into solid tumours; only if all of these checkpoints are blocked does the firepower of the T cells return, and current drugs mainly target the two lines of CTLA-4 and PD-1/PD-L1, so solid tumours need several approaches at once. The other three are the immunosuppressive cytokine, the cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the surrounding immune attack, and tumour-associated macrophages.

questions.q: First you circle out a morphologically uniform region under the microscope (a pure tumour nest, for example), then cut it out with a laser and transfer it to another slide; this technique is called ____.
options: FACS
Immunofluorescence (IF)
Flow cytometry
Laser capture microdissection (LCM)
questions.why: The point of LCM is to separate physically what you want from what you do not: a tumour specimen contains not only cancer cells but also cancer-associated fibroblasts, immune cells and extracellular matrix, and all of these contribute protein signal, so a morphologically uniform region is cut out to avoid contaminating the specimen with stromal and immune cells. The other three are the machine that sorts cells into different tubes according to fluorescence, the method of staining tissue with fluorescently labelled antibodies, and the instrument that measures cell size and fluorescence.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term linker correspond to?
options: The hydrophobic stretch of a protein that sits in the membrane; remove it and the protein dissolves into the water, so it can be measured in blood.
A short linking peptide that joins two protein segments together.
The smallest usable fragment of an antibody: one heavy-chain variable region plus one light-chain variable region.
fibroblast activation protein - the marker on the surface of activated fibroblasts.
questions.why: In an scFv the linker joins the antibody's heavy-chain VH to the light-chain VL, turning them into a single expressible protein while preserving the original antigen-binding ability; in an ADC it joins the antibody to the payload, and changing to a branched linker allows two drugs to be carried at once; its length and flexibility also affect whether the whole scFv folds correctly. The other three are the hydrophobic stretch of a protein that sits in the membrane, the variable region fragment of an antibody, and the marker on the surface of activated fibroblasts.

questions.q: The lipid vesicle that wraps up mRNA and uses the lipid properties of the cell membrane to deliver the cargo into the cell is called which of the following in English?
options: FACS
Ex vivo
Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)
linker
questions.why: mRNA injected on its own is broken down immediately and cannot get into the cell; the LNP wraps the mRNA up and uses the lipid properties of the cell membrane to deliver the cargo, and after entry into the endosome the mRNA is released for the ribosome to translate. In the design of in vivo CAR-T, the mRNA encodes a fragment of an anti-CD5 antibody, which recognises the T cell and delivers the CAR mRNA into it. The other three are the machine that sorts cells according to fluorescence, handling cells outside the body, and the short peptide that joins two protein segments together.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Liquid biopsy correspond to?
options: Looking for tumour material in a blood sample instead of cutting a piece out of the tumour.
Cancer cells that have shed from the tumour and are travelling in the blood.
Cutting a clean region out of a tissue section under the microscope, avoiding contamination by other cells.
The scaffold of proteins and sugars in which cells sit and which they must dig through to move.
questions.why: A solid tumour continually sheds cancer cells into the blood, and these circulating tumour cells can be separated from the white blood cells as EpCAM-positive and CD45-negative and then have their DNA sequenced; a doctor can therefore track the disease by taking blood repeatedly instead of asking the patient to undergo biopsy or scanning again. Note that a CTC may already have been through EMT, so its markers do not match the primary tumour, and patients with CTC 5 or more have the worst survival. The other three are the cancer cells that have shed from the tumour and are travelling in the blood, cutting a clean region out of tissue with a laser, and that extracellular scaffold of proteins and sugars.

questions.q: Why does he say that when reading a KM curve you should ask whether 'the two lines can be separated'?
options: The statistical test that compares two survival curves and calculates a p value.
The survival time during which the disease has not progressed further.
The group of patients with no circulating tumour cells at all in their blood.

What the log-rank test compares is not the survival rate at a single time point but the degree to which the two curves separate overall; a small p value means that the separation of the two curves is unlikely to be random fluctuation.
questions.why: He writes the result of the log-rank test straight onto the figure, for instance P<0.001 on the dMMR versus pMMR graph; what the log-rank test compares is the degree of overall separation of the two curves, putting the time at which each patient had the event and whether they were censored into the model to see whether the difference between the two groups accumulates over time. The other three are the test itself, the survival time that looks only at whether the tumour progresses, and the group of patients with no circulating tumour cells in their blood.

questions.q: Drawing blood from the patient to take T cells, introducing the CAR with a virus or electroporation, growing millions of CAR-T cells, infusing them back into the patient and then observing the tumour response - what is this process called in English?
options: Ex vivo
manufacturing cycle
Liquid biopsy
Adoptive cell therapy
questions.why: His slide lists these five steps: draw blood from the patient to take T cells, introduce the CAR with a virus or electroporation, grow out millions of CAR-T cells, infuse them back into the patient, and then wait a while to see the tumour response; the whole procedure is the source of the cost and time of autologous CAR-T, and the reason behind the US$370,000 to US$475,000 per course of treatment - the more steps there are, and the more each of them has to be handled in a sterile environment, the greater the time and the cost. The other three are the concept of handling cells outside the body, looking for tumour material in a blood sample, and the overall strategy of removing, modifying and returning cells to fight the tumour.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term MCP-1 correspond to?
options: fibroblast activation protein - the marker on the surface of activated fibroblasts.
Grab it and the white blood cell can squeeze out between two cells and leave the vessel.
The chemokine that draws white blood cells to a particular place.
The cell-surface protein that makes white blood cells roll along the vessel wall.
questions.why: Chemokines are the dispatch signals between cells, and MCP-1 is the call-up among them; it is responsible for the last step of leukocyte extravasation: first P-selectin, E-selectin and integrin make the white blood cell roll, then ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 provide adhesion and activation, then PECAM-1 carries it through the vessel wall, and finally it follows the concentration gradient of MCP-1 towards the site of inflammation. The other three are the marker on the surface of activated fibroblasts, the molecule that lets white blood cells squeeze out of the vessel wall, and the surface protein that makes them roll along the vessel wall.

questions.q: A single staining that lets you see several targets at once, for example the positions of the Hippo pathway members MST1, LATS and YAP within the same cell; this method, in which each target is given its own antibody in a different fluorescent colour, is called ____.
options: Multiplex immunofluorescence
Immunofluorescence (IF)
Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
Confocal microscopy
questions.why: Giving each target its own antibody carrying a different fluorescent dye means that one staining shows several targets at once, for example whether the Hippo pathway members MST1, LATS and YAP sit in the same cell; DAPI stains the nucleus blue to give a coordinate frame, and confocal then stacks different focal planes to rebuild the three dimensions, something wide-field IF cannot do - and in the tumour microenvironment, where cancer cells, immune cells and fibroblasts are all mixed together, exactly this resolving power is needed. The other three are the broad concept of staining tissue with fluorescently labelled antibodies, the method that leaves a coloured deposit with an enzyme substrate, and the microscope that focuses on one thin optical section at a time.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Neoantigen correspond to?
options: Cells whose mutation rate has been pushed to an extreme level.
A tumour carrying a large load of neoantigens; it responds well to immunotherapy.
deficient mismatch repair - mismatch repair deficiency.
Protein fragments the immune system has never seen, usually produced by frameshifts or novel splice sites.
questions.why: Ordinary protein fragments were long ago recorded by the immune system as one's own, so they are not attacked; a neoantigen is instead a product distorted by mutation: a frameshift shifts the whole sequence out of register and attaches a strange stretch, while a novel splice site makes the protein gain or lose a segment and look different, and once these fragments are presented by MHC the cytotoxic T cells recognise them and attack. The other three are the cell with the mutation rate pushed to the extreme, the hot tumour carrying a large load of neoantigen, and the pathological shorthand for defective mismatch repair.

questions.q: Which of the following in English is the member of the selectin family alongside E-selectin and L-selectin that is stored in granules, moves rapidly to the cell surface on activation, and is expressed by both platelets and endothelium?
options: E-selectin
P-selectin
Selectin
PECAM-1
questions.why: The selectins have three members: E-selectin (expressed by vascular endothelial cells after inflammatory stimulation), P-selectin (expressed by both platelets and endothelium, stored in granules and moved rapidly to the surface on activation) and L-selectin (expressed by the white blood cells themselves); their shared job is to make white blood cells roll along the vascular endothelium, and the cell must slow down in this first step before the adhesion of the second step can proceed. The other three are the selectin expressed in large amounts on endothelium only during inflammation, the family name selectin itself, and the molecule that lets white blood cells pass out of the vessel wall.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term PD-1 correspond to?
options: A protein on tumour cells that binds PD-1 and switches T cells off.
PD-L2, the second ligand of PD-1.
A checkpoint receptor on T cells; once PD-L1 binds it, the T cell is switched off.
The state in which a tumour escapes attack because the T cells have been switched off.
questions.why: PD-1 is an inhibitory receptor on the surface of T cells, normally there to prevent excessive T-cell activation; tumour cells exploit it by expressing PD-L1 on their surface, and once PD-L1 binds PD-1 the T cell enters anergy and its attacking firepower is switched off - the commonest trick in tumour immune evasion, and blocking it amounts to removing the brake. The other three are the PD-L1 protein on tumour cells, the second ligand of PD-1, and the overall state in which a tumour escapes attack.

questions.q: His HDAC inhibitor slide says that RGFP 966 raises PD-L1 through BRD4 and thereby makes the tumour more sensitive to blockade; what does he call this phenomenon?
options: His HDAC inhibitor slide shows that RGFP 966 raises PD-L1 through BRD4 and thereby makes the tumour more sensitive to blockade; this is what he calls gene addiction.
A tumour with few neoantigens, which responds poorly to checkpoint inhibitors.
A tumour carrying a large load of neoantigens; it responds well to immunotherapy.
The cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the immune attack around it.
questions.why: Other drugs in the same HDAC inhibitor group, such as ricolinostat and citarinostat, make the tumour easier to kill, whereas RGFP 966 raises CTL activity. This gene addiction also explains why a cold tumour can be induced by an HDAC inhibitor to express PD-L1 and so be converted into a hot tumour. The other three are the cold tumour with few neoantigens that responds poorly to checkpoint inhibitors, the hot tumour that responds well to immunotherapy, and the cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the surrounding immune attack.

questions.q: Which of the following in English is the ligand for PD-1 that is expressed mainly on dendritic cells and macrophages, listed alongside PD-L1 but coming from a different source in the tumour microenvironment?
options: PD-1
PD-L1
CTLA-4
PD-L2
questions.why: Both PD-L1 and PD-L2 can bind PD-1 on T cells, and once PD-1 is engaged the T cell enters anergy and loses its attacking power; PD-L2 is expressed mainly on dendritic cells and macrophages and is the second source of inhibitory signalling in the tumour microenvironment, and his list places PD-L1 and PD-L2 side by side to show that a tumour can reach the same brake through different molecules. The other three are the inhibitory receptor on T cells, that ligand on tumour cells, and the checkpoint receptor that competes with CD28 for the same B7.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term PECAM-1 correspond to?
options: The chemokine that draws white blood cells to a particular place.
Grab it and the white blood cell can squeeze out between two cells and leave the vessel.
The adhesion molecule that lets white blood cells hold on to the vessel wall tightly.
The cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the immune attack around it.
questions.why: Leukocyte extravasation has four steps: P-selectin and E-selectin make the cell roll; ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 make it stick and become activated; PECAM-1 (CD31) forms a 'door' at the junctions between cells of the vessel wall, and the white blood cell squeezes through it once it grabs hold; finally it follows the MCP-1 gradient towards its target. All four steps are indispensable and their order cannot be changed. The other three are the chemokine that attracts white blood cells, the adhesion molecule on activated endothelium, and the cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the surrounding immune attack.

questions.q: When killer T cells and NK cells kill a target cell, the granules fuse with the cell membrane and release ____, which punches a hole in the membrane so that granzyme can enter the target cell.
options: Granzyme
Complement
Perforin
EpCAM
questions.why: The killing by killer T cells and NK cells takes three steps: after recognising the target, the granules move towards it and fuse with the cell membrane, releasing perforin; perforin punches a hole in the membrane and the granzymes pass through it into the target cell; the granzymes then start the caspase cascade and the target cell undergoes apoptosis. Perforin is only responsible for opening the door - granzyme carries out the death sentence - and CAR-T uses the same route. The other three are the enzyme that kills the target cell after entering it, the group of plasma proteins that can attack cells on their own, and the surface protein used to sift out tumour cells.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term pinhole correspond to?
options: The small aperture in a confocal microscope that blocks out-of-focus light.
A microscope that focuses on one thin optical section at a time, used to pinpoint labelled proteins.
Two proteins found in the same place in the same cell, demonstrated by overlapping fluorescent staining.
A fluorescent dye that glows blue and specifically stains nuclei.
questions.why: An ordinary fluorescence microscope illuminates the whole field, so the upper and lower layers of a thick cell all light up and overlap; confocal places a pinhole in front of the detector so that only light from the focal plane gets through, which allows optical sections to be taken layer by layer, and stacking these sections gives the 3D reconstruction; the size of the pinhole determines how thin the section is, the smaller the aperture the higher the axial resolution. The other three are the confocal microscope itself, the co-localisation of proteins, and the blue dye that stains nuclei.

questions.q: The kind of survival time that in a trial looks only at whether the tumour has progressed and not at whether the patient has died, is called which of the following in English?
options: EpCAM
PD-L2
Log-rank test
progression-free survival
questions.why: Unlike median overall survival, PFS does not look at whether the patient has died, only at whether the tumour has progressed, and in trials it usually shows a difference between groups earlier than overall survival does, which is why it is often used for early reads; the y axis of his MSI-H versus pMMR graph is precisely progression-free survival, and 'the MSI-H/MMR-deficient group is clearly better on the PFS curve' is the figure he calls 'one of the most important graphs in modern medicine'. The other three are the surface protein used to sift out tumour cells, the second ligand of PD-1, and the statistical test that compares two survival curves and calculates a p value.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term rolling correspond to?
options: The surface protein used to pick tumour cells out of a blood sample.
The first step, in which immune cells roll along the inner wall of the blood vessel.
The step in which immune cells pass through the vessel wall into the tissue.
The step in which immune cells roll up to the vessel wall and then adhere and are activated.
questions.why: As the blood flows, white blood cells roll along the vessel wall through repeated binding and unbinding between P-selectin, E-selectin and integrin; this step is slow, and its purpose is to give the cell a chance to stop in the right place and move on to the adhesion and activation that follow - and many tumour microenvironment problems arise precisely because this step is too inefficient. The other three are the surface protein used to sift out tumour cells, the step of passing through the vessel wall into tissue, and the adhesion and activation that follow rolling.

questions.q: Why does a CAR keep only the scFv of the antibody and discard the Fc half?
options: The smallest usable fragment of an antibody: one heavy-chain variable region plus one light-chain variable region.
A short linking peptide that joins two protein segments together.
The Fc half is responsible for communicating with the immune system, whereas all a CAR wants is the single function of 'grabbing antigen', so only the antigen-binding scFv is kept.
An artificial receptor fitted onto a T cell so that it recognises a tumour protein and kills that cell.
questions.why: The Y-shaped tip of an antibody is the antigen-binding site, made up of the two variable domains VH of the heavy chain and VL of the light chain; joining these two with a short peptide gives the scFv, which can be expressed as a single polypeptide, and the rest of the antibody can be discarded, because the Fc half is responsible for communicating with the immune system while all a CAR wants is the single function of 'grabbing antigen'. The other three are the scFv fragment itself, the short peptide that links the two parts of an antibody, and the artificial receptor as a whole.

questions.q: The family of cell-surface proteins made up of E-selectin, P-selectin and L-selectin that provides the first step of white blood cells rolling along the vascular endothelium is called which of the following in English?
options: Selectin
rolling
PECAM-1
adhesion and activation
questions.why: The selectins have three members: E-selectin (expressed by vascular endothelial cells after inflammatory stimulation), P-selectin (expressed by both platelets and endothelium, stored in granules) and L-selectin (expressed by the white blood cells themselves); their shared job is to make white blood cells roll along the vascular endothelium, and the cell must slow down in this first step before the adhesion of the second step can proceed, after which ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 handle adhesion, PECAM-1 the passage through and MCP-1 the chemotaxis. The other three are the step of rolling itself, the molecule responsible for passing through the vessel wall, and the adhesion and activation step that follows rolling.

questions.q: His demonstration plot puts granulocytes at high SSC, monocytes in the middle and lymphocytes at low SSC; this scatter channel, which reflects the internal complexity of a cell, is called ____ in English.
options: Forward scatter (FSC)
granularity
Flow cytometry
side scatter (SSC)
questions.why: When light hits a cell it scatters not only forwards (reflecting size) but also sideways; the greater the sideways angle, the more 'messy' the inside of the cell and the more granules it contains, so granulocytes have a high SSC and lymphocytes a low one, while forward scatter roughly corresponds to cell size - and the two scatter axes together are like a 'weight and baggage' chart for a cell. The other three are the forward scatter channel that reflects cell size, the concept of granularity read out by side scatter, and the instrument that measures cell size and fluorescence.

questions.q: Macrophages that have been recruited and reprogrammed by the tumour, releasing VEGF to promote angiogenesis and also releasing PD-L1 to hold down T cells, are called ____.
options: Cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF)
TAMs
Tregs
CTLA-4
questions.why: TAMs are macrophages recruited and reprogrammed by the tumour, and they play a double role: on one hand they are used by the tumour, and on the other they release VEGF to promote angiogenesis while also releasing PD-L1 and cytokines that hold T cells down; in his tumour microenvironment list TAMs stand alongside Treg and MDSC as the group that suppresses immunity. The other three are cancer-associated fibroblasts, regulatory T cells, and the checkpoint receptor that competes with CD28 for the same B7.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term TGFβ correspond to?
options: A cytokine that suppresses the immune response.
The cytokine that comes after IFN-γ in the NF-κB response and keeps NK cells alive.
The cytokine the tumour uses to dampen the immune attack around it.
An enzyme that deprives T cells of the amino acid they need, shutting them down.
questions.why: TGFβ is originally a signal that regulates cell growth, repair and immunity, but in the tumour microenvironment it is hijacked into an immunosuppressant: it inhibits the activity of effector T cells, promotes the expansion of Tregs, and works together with MDSC - his third-lecture slide shows MDSC secreting TGF-β, IL-10 and PD-L1 to suppress CD8+ T cells. The other three are the immunosuppressive cytokine, the cytokine that keeps NK cells alive, and the enzyme that breaks down tryptophan and leaves T cells short of food.

questions.q: His slide 63 sets out the inhibitory checkpoints as a list: besides CTLA-4, PD-1, LAG3 and VISTA, the fifth on the list is ____.
options: TIM3
PD-L2
VISTA
LAG3
questions.why: TIM3, like CTLA-4, PD-1, LAG3 and VISTA, is listed on his slide 63 among the inhibitory checkpoints, and all of them sit on the surface of effector T cells; when the tumour environment supplies its ligand, the activity of the T cell is pushed down. His point is that CAR-T works in blood cancers but is held up in solid tumours by this whole row of brakes, so solid tumours need several approaches at once. The other three are the second ligand of PD-1, the inhibitory checkpoint that sits at the interface between immune cells and tumour cells, and the inhibitory checkpoint receptor that is a T-cell brake alongside PD-1.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Transmembrane domain correspond to?
options: The flexible connecting segment between the DNA-binding domain and the ligand-binding domain of a nuclear receptor.
The scaffold of proteins and sugars in which cells sit and which they must dig through to move.
fibroblast activation protein - the marker on the surface of activated fibroblasts.
The hydrophobic stretch of a protein that sits in the membrane; remove it and the protein dissolves into the water, so it can be measured in blood.
questions.why: A transmembrane region is an α-helix or β-barrel rich in hydrophobic amino acids and long enough to span the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane; a receptor such as HER2 uses it to connect the extracellular portion with the intracellular kinase domain. The alternative splicing application in the fifth lecture is to splice out the transmembrane region, which turns the protein into a soluble isoform so that it appears in blood or urine and can be measured as a biomarker. The other three are the connecting segment between the two functional domains of a nuclear receptor, that extracellular scaffold of proteins and sugars, and the marker on the surface of activated fibroblasts.

questions.q: Why is membrane proteomics regarded as the hardest part of proteomics?
options: The hydrophobic stretch of a protein that sits in the membrane; remove it and the protein dissolves into the water, so it can be measured in blood.

The amino acids of a transmembrane segment are not water-soluble, so detergent or lipid has to surround them for them to stay in solution - and these reagents themselves then interfere with the measurement.
The scaffold of proteins and sugars in which cells sit and which they must dig through to move.
The surface protein used to pick tumour cells out of a blood sample.
questions.why: The amino acids of a transmembrane segment are all hydrophobic and unfriendly to water, and ordinary mass spectrometry has to measure proteins in aqueous solution, so such proteins precipitate before they even reach the instrument; the solution is to add detergent or lipid, but those molecules then interfere with the measurement itself, which is why membrane proteomics became the hardest part of proteomics. The other three are the function of the transmembrane region and the application of splicing it into a soluble version, the extracellular matrix scaffold, and the marker used to sift out tumour cells.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term transmigration correspond to?
options: The first step, in which immune cells roll along the inner wall of the blood vessel.
The step in which immune cells roll up to the vessel wall and then adhere and are activated.
The step in which immune cells pass through the vessel wall into the tissue.
Cells moving along a chemical concentration gradient.
questions.why: After rolling and adhesion, the immune cell has to find a place in the vessel wall to squeeze out through, and that is what molecules such as PECAM-1 are for; only after passing through does it enter the fourth step, chemotaxis, moving along the chemical gradient towards the tumour, and every step is a point at which treatment can intervene - blocking a chemokine receptor, for example, lets the cells arrive but not gather. The other three are the rolling of the first step, the adhesion and activation that follow rolling, and moving along a chemical concentration gradient.

questions.q: The group of T cells that normally prevents the immune system from attacking the body's own tissues, but which the tumour induces to expand so as to suppress effector T cells, is called which of the following in English?
options: Tregs
TAMs
LAG3
Cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF)
questions.why: Tregs are a group of T cells dedicated to suppressing the immune response, which in normal circumstances stop the immune system attacking the body's own tissues; inside a tumour they are put to work by the tumour, the microenvironment inducing Treg expansion to push down the effector T cells that target the tumour. His slide on the obstacles to CAR-T lists Tregs, MDSCs and TAMs alongside TGFβ and IL-10, and adds hypoxia, an acidic environment and a rich ECM, all of which together form the defensive works of a solid tumour. The other three are tumour-associated macrophages, an inhibitory checkpoint receptor, and cancer-associated fibroblasts.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term Tumor microenvironment correspond to?
options: Fibroblasts recruited and reprogrammed by the tumour, dedicated to building the surrounding stroma.
The scaffold of proteins and sugars in which cells sit and which they must dig through to move.
The tumour's whole neighbourhood: cancer cells, immune cells, fibroblasts and stroma together.
The change in which cells lose their grip on their neighbours and become free to move and invade.
questions.why: His definition is explicit: tumour = cancer cells + immune cells + CAFs + ECM; the cancer cells are responsible for proliferation, immune cells can either help or be turned, the CAFs make the matrix and the ECM forms the solid barrier, and the tumour remodels this environment to protect itself, producing TGFβ and IL-10, inducing Tregs and MDSCs, and expressing PD-L1 to put effector T cells into anergy. The other three are the fibroblasts that build the matrix, that scaffold woven from proteins and sugars, and the change by which epithelial cells become mesenchymal.

questions.q: When the proofreading exonuclease activity of Pol ε is lost and the error rate of replication rises sharply, the cell becomes an ____; his Kaplan-Meier curves show the prognosis of the POLE-mutant group to be better than that of the wild-type group.
options: dMMR
ultramutator
CTC0
Neoantigen
questions.why: When the proofreading exonuclease activity of the polymerase is lost and the replication error rate rises sharply, the cell becomes an ultramutator; on the surface this looks worse, but the result is better, because the neoantigen load rises, tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes increase and the patient's prognosis improves - the most counter-intuitive conclusion of the fourth lecture: the most mutated tumours are the ones the immune system sees most clearly, so treatment works best on them. The other three are the pathological shorthand for defective mismatch repair, the group of patients with no circulating tumour cells in their blood, and protein fragments the immune system has never seen.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term VCAM-1 correspond to?
options: One of the selectins, which makes white blood cells roll along the vessel wall.
Grab it and the white blood cell can squeeze out between two cells and leave the vessel.
The adhesion molecule that lets white blood cells hold on to the vessel wall tightly.
The chemokine that draws white blood cells to a particular place.
questions.why: The four steps of leukocyte extravasation are rolling (via selectins), adhesion/activation (via ICAM-1 and VCAM-1), transmigration (via PECAM-1) and chemotaxis (via MCP-1); VCAM-1 is expressed on activated vascular endothelium and binds the integrin on white blood cells, catching the rolling cell and flattening it in preparation for passage, and its soluble form is shed and can be measured in blood. The other three are one of the selectins responsible for rolling, the molecule that lets white blood cells squeeze out of the vessel wall, and the chemokine that attracts white blood cells.

questions.q: The inhibitory checkpoint listed on his slide 63 that is expressed mainly on myeloid cells and tumour cells and for which no mature targeted drug yet exists, is called which of the following in English?
options: VISTA
TIM3
LAG3
PD-L2
questions.why: VISTA is one of the inhibitory checkpoints listed on his slide 63 (CTLA-4, PD-1, LAG3, TIM3 and VISTA are all on the effector cell side, while PD-L1 and PD-L2 are on the target cell side); what distinguishes it from the other checkpoints is that it is expressed mainly on myeloid cells and tumour cells, that it has only in recent years been recognised as an important target, and that no mature targeted drug exists for it yet. The other three are TIM3 and LAG3, likewise listed as inhibitory checkpoints, and the second ligand of PD-1.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does the English term ZAP70 correspond to?
options: An artificial receptor fitted onto a T cell so that it recognises a tumour protein and kills that cell.
The segment inside a CAR that delivers the second signal and fully switches the T cell on.
The enzyme that kills the target cell after entering it.
The kinase that carries the signal inside the CAR.
questions.why: The structure of a CAR has three parts: the extracellular scFv (which recognises antigen), the hinge and transmembrane region in between, and the intracellular signalling tail; the tail usually contains CD3 zeta and ZAP70, and when the scFv grabs hold of the antigen the tail passes the signal into the interior of the T cell and starts off a cascade of phosphorylation reactions - without this link a CAR is merely a light sensor. The other three are the artificial receptor as a whole, the intracellular co-stimulatory segment, and the enzyme that kills the target cell after entering it.
